name.text: Middle High German nam, name, Old High German namo, Germanic *naman-, Indo-European *enmen-/enomen-/*nomen-, recorded since the 8th century.

nachname.text: Compound of the preposition nach and the noun Name.

adresse.text: In the sense “postal address”, borrowed in the 17th century from French adresse “direction, direct route”. In the sense “a written document addressed to a high-ranking person”, the word was borrowed in the 18th century from English address.

strasse.text: Middle High German „strāze“, Old High German „strāza“, borrowed from Latin „via strata“ = “paved road”. The word is recorded since the 8th century. It goes back further to Latin stratus, the past participle of the verb sternere “to stretch out, to spread, to cover with a layer”.

stadt.text: Middle High German stat, Old High German stat “place, site”, recorded since the 8th century; in today’s sense “place where many people live” since the 13th century.

land.text: Inherited word from Middle High German lant, which goes back to Old High German lant, which in turn can be traced back to Proto-Germanic *landa- ‘open land, heath’.

telefonnummer.text: Compound of the nouns Telefon and Nummer.

alter.text: Noun formed from the adjective alt.

beruf.text: From Middle High German beruof (“reputation”), used by Luther for »calling« (for Greek κλῆσις, Latin vocatio). It was then also used for »a person’s station and office« (related to berufen).

sprache.text: Middle High German sprāche “language”, Old High German sprāhha, West Germanic *sprǣku “language”, recorded since the 8th century.

herr.text: Recorded since the 8th century; Middle High German hēr, a form of address from hērre ‘ruler, patron saint, noble vassal, nobleman’, from Old High German hērro ‘ruler, feudal lord’. This is shortened from the comparative used as a noun, hēríro, hērōro ‘the older one, the more worthy one; older, more venerable’. It belongs to the basic form hēr ‘old, venerable’, which gave hehr; see there.

gloss.Höhergestellter, Ranghöchster: person of higher rank, highest in rank

frau.text: Middle High German vrouwe from Old High German frouwa “lady, mistress” from the 9th century, related to frō “lord”; originally these were forms of address for gods.

mann.text: Middle High German and Old High German „man“, recorded since the 8th century; originally probably “thinking being” or “being that walks upright”.

person.text: The noun Person has been part of the standard vocabulary since the 12th century: Middle High German persōn, persōne, borrowed from Latin persona “mask, role, character [of an actor]”. The Latin persōna probably comes in turn from Etruscan persuh “mask”.

familie.text: Borrowed in the 15th century from Latin familia = servants, household.

mutter.text: Middle High German muoter, Old High German muoter, Germanic *mōder-, Indo-European *mátēr “mother”; the word is recorded in German since the 8th century.

vater.text: Old High German fater, from Germanic *fader, from Indo-European *pH2tér (pronounced roughly: pchtér, with “ch” as in “ach”).

kind.text: Middle High German kint, Old High German kind, Germanic *kinþa-, originally from the Proto-Indo-European root *g’enə- “to give life”; recorded since the 8th century.

sohn.text: From Indo-European *seu, *sū > to give birth, to reproduce <. Germanic: sunuz, Old English: sunu, Old Frisian: sunu, Old Saxon: sunu, Old High German: sunu, Old Norse: sonr, Gothic: sunus.

tochter.text: Middle High German tohter, Old High German tohter, from Germanic *„duhter-“. It is an inherited Indo-European word, also related to Greek θυγάτηρ “daughter”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

bruder.text: Middle High German bruoder, Old High German bruodar (related to Gothic broþar), Germanic brōþēr “brother”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

schwester.text: From Middle High German and Old High German ‚swester‘, from Germanic ‚*swester-‘ “sister”, Indo-European ‚*su̯esor-‘ “sister, female relative”, recorded since the 8th century.

grossvater.text: Compound of the adjective groß and the noun Vater.

oma.text: A child’s shortening of Großmama; an in-between form was Omama.

opa.text: A child’s shortening of Großpapa; an in-between form was Opapa.

onkel.text: Borrowed around 1700 via (Old) French oncle, with the same meaning, from Latin avunculus (“mother’s brother”).

tante.text: Borrowed in the 18th century from French tante, with the same meaning.

cousin.text: Borrowed in the 17th century from French cousin, which goes back to Classical Latin consobrinus (“children of siblings, in relation to each other”).

ehefrau.text: Compound of the nouns Ehe and Frau.

freund.text: Middle High German vriunt, Old High German friunt, from Proto-Germanic *frijōnd-, recorded since the 8th century.

baby.text: Borrowed in the 19th century from English baby.

gefuehl.text: Formed from the stem of the verb fühlen with the prefix ge-.

angst.text: Recorded since the 8th century; Old High German angust; Middle High German angest; from West Germanic *angusti- “fear”, related to the adjective *angu- “being narrow”; this in turn comes from the Indo-European root *angʰu- “narrow, pressing”; compare Latin angustus “narrow” and Old Indian aṁhah (stem: aṁhas-) “fear”.

freude.text: Recorded since the 8th/9th century; Middle High German vröude, vreude, Old High German frewida, frouwida, Proto-Germanic *frawiþō-, also Low German Fraid; an abstract noun from *frawaz, which gave froh; more there.

liebe.text: An abstract noun from the adjective lieb, formed from the Old High German words liubī (9th century) and lioba (11th century), which became liebe in Middle High German. It meant pleasure in or through something, being dear or loving, favour and kindness.

glueck.text: Middle Low German gelükke, lükke, of unknown origin; Middle High German gelücke, glücke “fate”, recorded since the 12th century.

stress.text: From English stress “tension, pressure, strain, demand”. The term was introduced in 1936 by the Austrian biochemist Hans Selye (1907–1982), who worked at McGill University in Montreal (Canada).

spass.text: Borrowed in the 17th century from Italian spasso “amusement”.

problem.text: Borrowed in the 16th century from Latin problema (an undecided, doubtful task set to be solved; a disputed question), which goes back to Greek πρόβλημα “task, disputed question”.

lust.text: Middle High German lust, Old High German lust, Germanic *lustu- “wish, desire”, recorded since the 8th century.

haus.text: This is an inherited word recorded since the 8th century. Its Old High German form was hūs, and it meant the ‘building’ as well as the ‘family’, the ‘household’ and the ‘lineage’.

wohnung.text: Origin: Middle High German wonunge, Old High German wonunga, “stay, remaining, area, habit”, recorded since the 9th century.

zimmer.text: Middle High German zimber, zimer, zimmer, Old High German zimbar “building timber, wooden building, living space, dwelling”, Germanic *temra- “building timber, something built of wood”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

gloss.Bauholz, Gezimmertes: building timber, something built of wood

kueche.text: The word is recorded since the 9th century (around 800). Its Old High German form was kuhhina (compare Old English cycene), and its Middle High German forms were küchen / kuchen and küche / kuche (compare Middle Low German koke / kȫke, kokene / kȫkene / kȫken; Middle Dutch cokene, cuekene).

bad.text: Middle High German bat, Old High German bad, recorded since the 8th century; the earlier origin is not certain.

schlafzimmer.text: Compound of the stem of the verb schlafen and Zimmer.

wohnzimmer.text: Compound of the stem of the verb wohnen and Zimmer.

kinderzimmer.text: Compound of the nouns Kind and Zimmer, with the linking element -er.

flur.text: In the sense “hallway”, the word was only taken over from Low German in modern times; according to Duden, since around 1700.

balkon.text: The noun was borrowed at the end of the 17th century from French balcon, which comes from Italian balcone ‘loft; scaffold; balcony’, an enlarged form of Italian balco.

garten.text: Via Middle High German garte, the word goes back to the Old High German masculine noun garto (weak declension), recorded since the 8th century. In Middle High German, starting in the 15th century, the word takes the final -n from the other cases into the nominative, which gives modern German Garten.

keller.text: Middle High German keller, Old High German kellari, keller, kelre; borrowed in the 8th century from Latin cellarium “pantry, storeroom”; formed from cella “cell”, “small storeroom”.

tuer.text: Middle High German „tür(e)“, Old High German „turi, tür“, Germanic *„dur-“, from Indo-European *„dhwer-“. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

fenster.text: Fenster goes back to Latin fenestra (‘hatch for lighting a room, opening’), which probably has Etruscan roots. It came via the Old High German words fenstar and the rare finestra and Middle High German venster (‘window niche, light hatch’); Dutch venster and Old English fenester come from the same source.

wand.text: Middle High German wand, Old High German wand, Germanic *wandu- “wickerwork, rod” (“the woven thing”, as opposed to a stone wall, compare winden), recorded since the 8th century.

boden.text: Middle High German bodem, boden, Old High German bodam, pre-German buþma- “ground”, recorded since the 9th century. According to Kluge, the word apparently goes back to an Indo-European *bud-men-.

decke.text: Middle High German decke, Old High German theckī, recorded since the 8th century.

treppe.text: Middle High German treppe or trappe “step” or “tread”, Old High German trappa “trap” or “snare”, recorded since the 12th century.

dach.text: From Middle High German dach, Old High German dah, literally = the thing that covers.

toilette.text: Borrowed in the 18th century from French toilette for “small cloth”; over time the meaning shifted from “cosmetics cloth” to getting dressed, to the clothes themselves and finally to “lavatory”.

miete.text: This is an inherited word recorded since the 8th century. Its Old High German form was miata ‘wage, gift’. In Middle High German this gave the forms miete and miet, both meaning ‘wage, reward, payback, talent, giving of gifts, bribery’ (compare Old Saxon mēda, Middle Low German mēde).

nachbar.text: Via Middle High German nāchgebūr(e) from Old High German nāhgibūr, which comes from West Germanic naehwa-gabūr(ōn) “neighbour”, made of naehwa “near” and ga-būra- “fellow resident of the village community”. The word is recorded since the 8th century, in its present form since the 14th century.

tisch.text: From Middle High German tisch, Old High German tisc, recorded since the 8th century, which comes from Latin discus (“bowl”), which in turn goes back to Greek diskos (“disc”).

stuhl.text: Middle High German stuol, Old High German stuol, Germanic *stōla-. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

bett.text: Middle High German bett, bette, Old High German betti (related to Gothic badi), Germanic *badja- “bed”, recorded since the 8th century.

schrank.text: From late Middle High German schrank (= closed-off room or (barred) frame), from Middle High German schranc, from Old High German scranc (= crossing, interweaving); related to schränken. The word is recorded since the 9th century.

sofa.text: Borrowed in the 17th century from French sofa and Italian sofa, which are based on Arabic suffa صُفَّة = piece of furniture for resting.

sessel.text: Middle High German sezzel, Old High German sezzal, related to Middle Low German setel, from Germanic *set-la- “seat”, recorded since the 9th century.

regal.text: The word is recorded since the 17th century; its origin is unclear.

lampe.text: From Middle High German lampe, borrowed from Old French lampe, which is probably based on Vulgar Latin lampada, or on the accusative form lampada (taken into Latin from Greek) of Latin lampas ‘torch, light, lamp stand’.

teppich.text: Middle High German tepich, (teppich), Old High German tepih, (teppih), from Latin tapetum, with the same meaning. Earlier origin: via Greek τάπης / ταπίς, probably borrowed from South Asian languages. The word is recorded since the 9th century.

spiegel.text: Middle High German spiegel, Old High German spiegal, spēgal, borrowed in the 8th century from Latin speculum “mirror”, a noun from Latin specere “to see” (compare spekulieren, Spektakel, Spekulatius).

kuehlschrank.text: Compound of the stem of the verb kühlen and the noun Schrank.

herd.text: Middle High German hert, “stove, hearth”, also “house, home”, Old High German herd “fireplace, ground (as a place for fire)”, recorded since the 9th century.

waschmaschine.text: Compound of the stem of the verb waschen and Maschine.

topf.text: The word comes from East Central German and spread further through Luther’s translation of the Bible. Its original source is unclear; it may be related to tief.

pfanne.text: Middle High German pfanne, Old High German pfanna, borrowed in the 9th century from Late Latin panna, which goes back via Latin pantina to Greek πατάνη “bowl”.

teller.text: Middle High German teller, teler, borrowed in the 13th century from Old French tailleor “serving plate”, which goes back in the end to Latin talea “cut-off, stick-shaped piece”. A Teller was originally something on which food was cut up.

glas.text: Middle High German „glas“, Old High German „glas“, West Germanic „*glas-“ “glass”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

tasse.text: The word is recorded since the 16th century. It was first borrowed as Upper German tatse from Italian tazza “drinking bowl” and later adapted to French tasse. The Romance forms come from Arabic طاس, which goes back to Persian ‎طشت‎‎.

messer.text: Middle High German mezzer, Old High German mezzisahs, mezzirahs, mezzer, mezzeres, West Germanic matiz-sahsa- (Germanic *mat- ‘food, meal’, Germanic *sahs- “short sword, knife”) in the sense “cutting tool for food”, recorded since the 8th century.

gabel.text: Middle High German gabel(e), Old High German gabala, West Germanic gablō “fork”, West Indo-European (in Europe) *gablo- “fork”, recorded since the 9th century.

loeffel.text: Middle High German leffel, Old High German leffil, a tool noun from the lost Old High German verb laffan, Middle High German laffen. It is based on Indo-European *lab(h), *lap(h) “to lick with slurping, smacking sounds”. The word is recorded since the 9th century.

handtuch.text: Middle High German hanttuoch, Old High German hanttuoh, recorded in a 12th-century manuscript.

seife.text: From Middle High German seife, Old High German seiffa, a word formed from seifa “resin”; at first it was a product for dyeing hair red. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

brot.text: Old High German brōt, Middle High German brōt, Old Saxon brōd, Old English brēad, Old French brād, Old Norse brauð; from Germanic *brauda-. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

broetchen.text: Diminutive of Brot with the suffix -chen; in northern and central Germany it became a word of its own.

butter.text: Via Middle High German buter, the word goes back to the (late) Old High German forms butera and butira, recorded since the 11th century.

kaese.text: Recorded since the 8th century; inherited word from Middle High German kæse, which goes back to Old High German kāsi (see also Old Saxon kiēsi, kēsi); like Old English cēse, it goes back to an early borrowing from Latin caseus “cheese”, which in turn belongs to a word for “fermentation”.

ei.text: Probably from Indo-European ōị-om, ōṷị-om (compare Ancient Greek ōon, ōion and Latin ovum), Indo-European əwei- – bird, in the sense of “the thing that belongs to the bird”; later also used for other animals and for the germ cell in general; from Germanic ajjam – egg; Old High German ei.

milch.text: From Middle High German milich and milch, from Old High German miluh, Proto-Germanic *meluks “milk”, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-; for how the word “Milch” is related to other Indo-European languages, see *h₂melǵ-. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

wasser.text: From Middle High German wazzer (compare Yiddish וואַסער), from Old High German wazzar, recorded since the 8th century.

kaffee.text: When coffee came to Germany from the Netherlands and Great Britain in the 17th century, it was still called Koffee; only in the 18th century did the O become an A, after the French word café had spread. In southern Germany it is still called that today.

tee.text: Tee was probably borrowed in the 17th century from southern Chinese (Amoy dialect) tē “tea”. It probably came into German through Dutch, where it is called thee.

saft.text: Middle High German „saft“, „saf“, Old High German „saf“, compare English „sap“; Indo-European „sap-“, „sab-“ = “to taste”.

bier.text: Middle High German bier, Old High German bior, West Germanic *beura- “beer”, recorded since the 9th century; the earlier origin is uncertain.

wein.text: The noun has been recorded in the German-speaking area since the 8th century (Middle High German, Old High German wīn). It is borrowed from Latin vinum, with the same meaning, which, together with Greek οἶνος (same meaning), may go back to a language of the Black Sea region.

fleisch.text: Middle High German vleisch, fleisch, Old High German fleisc, West Germanic *fleiska- “meat, flesh”, recorded since the 8th century.

fisch.text: Middle High German visch, Old High German fisc, from Germanic *fiska-, recorded since the 8th century; compare Old Saxon fisk, Old Norse fiskr, Old English fisc, Old Frankish fisk, Gothic fisks, Latin piscis.

gemuese.text: Middle High German gemüese for mash, a collective word from Mus, recorded since the 15th century.

obst.text: Middle High German obez, Old High German obaz, from *uba-ætaz, “side dish”, literally “food on top”, from ob, “to, in addition”, and az, “food”; compare Aas, essen. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

apfel.text: Apfel is a common Germanic word and probably first meant the crab apple. The German word developed via Middle High German apfel, from Old High German apful, from Proto-Germanic *apluz, from Proto-Indo-European *ab(e)l.

banane.text: In the 16th century, via Portuguese banana, from a Bantu language or a dialect of Guinea or the Congo.

kartoffel.text: Via the names Tartuffel and Tartüffel, still common in the 18th century, from Italian tartufolo, the diminutive of tartufo (truffle). The potato got this name because people confused it with the truffle, which also grows underground.

reis.text: Middle High German rīs, borrowed in the 14th century from Medieval Latin risum, risus, which goes back via Latin oriza, Greek ὄρυζα, ὄρυζον, and probably Iranian (Persian wrizey), in the end to Old Indian vrīhí-. This may be based on a Semitic word.

zucker.text: The word is recorded in German since the 13th century. Its Middle High German forms were zuker and zucker, which go back to the Old High German form zucker.

suppe.text: Taken over from Low German in the 14th century, with influence at the same time from French soupe.

salat.text: Borrowed in the 15th century from Italian insalata, from insalare, “to salt”, from sal, “salt”.

geld.text: Middle High German gelt, Old High German gelt “repayment, payment, income, value”, Germanic *geld-a- “repayment, compensation”, recorded since the 8th century; in the sense “minted means of payment” since the 14th century.

cent.text: Borrowed from English (or American) cent, via Middle French cent, from Latin centum.

preis.text: Borrowed in the 13th century from French prix, which goes back to Latin pretium ‘purchase price’. At first it meant ‘value’ and ‘praise’; from the 15th century, under Dutch influence, also ‘purchase price’.

kasse.text: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian cassa, with the same meaning; from Latin capsa = container, box; formed from the verb capere = to hold; compare Kapsel.

supermarkt.text: Borrowed from English supermarket; structurally: formed from Markt with the prefix super-.

markt.text: Middle High German market, markt, Old High German marcāt, borrowed from Late Latin marcātus, a variant of the Latin noun mercatus “purchase, market”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

geschaeft.text: From Middle High German gescheffede, geschefte, recorded since the 12th century. The word is an abstract noun from schaffen “to work”.

laden.text: Middle High German lade, laden “plank, board, window shutter, shop”, recorded since the 13th century; related to the word Latte.

baeckerei.text: Formed from Bäcker with the suffix -ei.

kunde.text: The word is recorded since the 8th century; Old High German kundo = announcer, witness; Middle High German kunde = ‘acquaintance, local person’; in the meaning given above since the 16th century; a noun formed from the adjective kund.

rechnung.text: Origin: Middle High German rechenunge, rechnunge, Old High German rehhanunga “order”, recorded since around the year 1000.

quittung.text: Late Middle High German quit(t)unge, recorded since the 15th century, from Middle High German quit “loose, free, released”, from Old French quite “free, released from an obligation, paid, settled”, from Latin quietus “calm, free from work and worry, undisturbed, secure, free”, from Latin quies “rest”.

tuete.text: Early New High German dute, dutte, thüte “something funnel-shaped or tube-shaped”, recorded since the 16th century; from Middle Low German tute “funnel-shaped thing” / Middle Dutch tute “funnel-shaped thing”; the earlier origin is unclear.

angebot.text: Noun formed from the verb anbieten by a change of the stem; since the 15th century in the form Anbot, since the end of the 18th century in today’s form, probably influenced by gebieten and Gebot.

liste.text: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian lista, which was taken from Medieval Latin lista (strip, edge) and is in the end of Germanic origin.

hose.text: Middle High German hose, Old High German hose, from Germanic *huson, a kind of stocking worn under the actual trousers (the Bruch); possibly from Greek kystis “bladder, small bag, tube”. The word is recorded since the 10th century.

hemd.text: Via Middle High German hem(e)de, Old High German hemidi, the word goes back to West Germanic *hamiÞja- “shirt”, recorded since the 8th century.

t-shirt.text: Borrowed from English T-shirt (a shirt in the shape of a T).

pullover.text: English pullover, literally “something pulled over”, from pull and over, literally “to pull over” or “to drag over”; recorded since the 1920s.

jacke.text: Borrowed in the 14th century as „jacca“ from French jaque, older jaque, jaque de mailles “soldier’s jerkin, mail shirt”.

mantel.text: From Old High German mantel with the same meaning, alongside mantal and mantil; Middle High German mantel and Middle Dutch mantel too. It was borrowed in the 11th century from Vulgar Latin mantellus “short cloak”, a diminutive of Latin mantus, which is probably of Celtic origin.

kleid.text: Recorded since the 12th century; Middle High German kleit; Middle Low German kled; compare Middle Dutch cleet, Old English clāþ, Old Icelandic klæði, Old Swedish klädhe; all originally meaning cloth; probably from the Indo-European root *glei- = to stick.

rock.text: Middle High German roc, rok, Old High German (h)roc, West Germanic *rukka- “skirt, coat”, recorded since the 9th century.

schuh.text: Middle High German schuoch, Old High German scouh, recorded since the 9th century, Gothic skōhs, from Indo-European *skō(u)ko- “covering (of the foot)”, related to Schote and Scheune.

socke.text: Middle High German soc(ke), Old High German soc, borrowed in the 9th century from Latin soccus “low shoe”.

muetze.text: From Medieval Latin almutium, almutia, meaning a cape over a clergyman’s shoulders and head, via Middle High German almuʒ, armuʒ and late Middle High German mutze, mütze. The word is recorded since the 14th century, in its present form since the 15th century.

schal.text: As Shawl, Schawl, Schaul (common spellings from the 18th to the early 20th century), borrowed in the 19th century from English shawl “wrap or headscarf”, which goes back to šāl “wrap”; the rarer 19th-century Schal probably comes from French châle.

handschuh.text: Middle High German hantschuoch, Old High German hantscuoh, recorded since the 9th century.

koerper.text: From Middle High German korper, borrowed from Latin corpus. It replaced Old High German līh and Middle High German līch, except in modern German Leiche.

kopf.text: Recorded since the 8th century; Old High German choph (Middle High German kopf) = ‘skull, bowl, drinking vessel’; borrowed from Latin cupa, cuppa = ‘cup’.

haar.text: Middle High German and Old High German hār, like Dutch haar, English hair, Swedish hår, from a Germanic *hēra- “hair”, from an Indo-European root *ker[s]- “to stand stiff, to be bristly”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

auge.text: Inherited word from Middle High German ouge, from Old High German ouga, from Proto-Germanic *ᚨᚢᚷᛟ (augô), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃okʷ- (“eye”).

ohr.text: Middle High German ōr(e), Old High German ōra, Germanic *auzōn, Indo-European *aus-. Compare Ancient Greek us, Latin auris and Russian ухо. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

nase.text: Middle High German nase, Old High German nasa, from Germanic *nas(ō) “nose”, from Indo-European *nas-, probably first meaning “nostril”, since dual and plural forms occur.

mund.text: Inherited word from Middle High German munt, Old High German mund, Germanic *munþa- “mouth”, recorded since the 8th century.

zahn.text: Old High German: zan; zand; zant.

hals.text: Middle High German hals, Old High German hals, Germanic *halsa- “neck”, recorded since the 8th century.

arm.text: Middle High German arm, Old High German ar(a)m, Germanic *arma- “arm”, from Indo-European arə “to join, to fit”; recorded since the 8th century.

hand.text: Middle High German „hant“, Old High German „hant“, Germanic *„handu-“ “hand”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

finger.text: Old High German and Old Saxon: fingar; Middle High German, Middle Low German and Dutch: vinger; Middle Dutch vingher; English and Swedish: finger; Old Norse: fingr; Gothic: figgrs. It comes either from Germanic *fengra, going back to the Indo-European number word *pénkʷe “five”, or from Germanic *fanhan “to grasp, to seize”, with a proposed Indo-European form *penkro-.

bein.text: Middle and Old High German bein, recorded since the 8th century. The origin of this old Germanic word is unclear.

fuss.text: Middle High German vuoჳ, Old High German fuoჳ, Germanic *fōt, Proto-Indo-European *pē̌d- or *pōd-, recorded since the 8th century; it is related to Old Saxon fōt, Middle Low German vōt, Middle Dutch and Dutch voet, Old English fōt and English foot.

ruecken.text: Middle High German rück(e), rügge, ruck(e), rugge, Old High German hruggi, ruggi, Germanic *hrugja-, recorded since the 8th century.

bauch.text: This is an inherited word from Old High German. It is recorded since the 8th century as part of the Old High German compound uuasbucho ‘a mutilated torso that was found’, and as a separate form būh since the 11th century (around 1000). In Middle High German it developed into the form būch.

herz.text: Middle High German hërz, hërze, Old High German hërza, Proto-Germanic *hertô “heart”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

gesicht.text: Middle High German gesiht and Old High German gisiht, recorded since the 8th century. The word is an abstract noun from sehen; today’s meaning developed from “sight, countenance”.

haut.text: Middle High German hūt, Old High German hūt, Germanic *hūdi- “skin”, recorded since the 8th century.

arzt.text: The noun Arzt comes from Old High German arzāt, from the 9th century, which replaced Old High German lāhhi, and from the Middle High German forms arzāt and arzet.

aerztin.text: Female form of Arzt, made with the suffix -in (plus an umlaut).

zahnarzt.text: Compound of the nouns Zahn and Arzt.

praxis.text: Borrowed from Latin praxis “exercise, method of proceeding”, which was borrowed from Ancient Greek praxis “doing, action, way of acting; reality”, from the verb πράσσειν “to do, to act”.

krankenhaus.text: Compound of the stem of the adjective used as a noun (ein) Kranker, the linking element -en and the noun Haus.

termin.text: Middle High German termin, borrowed in the 13th century from the Latin noun terminus (boundary).

wartezimmer.text: Compound of the stem of the verb warten and the noun Zimmer, with the linking sound -e-.

krankenkasse.text: Compound of the stem of Kranker, the linking element -en and Kasse.

tablette.text: Borrowed in the 18th century from French tablette “block, notebook”; the medical meaning only in the 20th century.

schmerz.text: Middle High German smerze, Old High German smerza, recorded since the 9th century; the word is probably an abstract noun from the West Germanic verb *smert-a- “to hurt”.

fieber.text: Middle High German fieber, vieber, Old High German fiebar, borrowed in the 9th century from Latin febris.

husten-noun.text: Middle High German huoste, Old High German huosto, huosta (9th century); related to Middle Low German hōst, hōste, Middle Dutch hoest, hoeste.

schnupfen.text: Noun made from the verb schnupfen without any ending.

erkaeltung.text: Noun formed from erkälten with the suffix -ung.

grippe.text: The word is recorded since the 18th century. It is borrowed from French grippe, which was first used with the French article as la grippe, then generally as Grippe from 1800.

rezept.text: From Latin recipe = “take” [the doctor’s instruction], and the following receptus = “received” [by the pharmacist]; both are forms of the verb recipere; compare rezipieren. The word is recorded since the 14th century.

unfall.text: Late Middle High German unval “misfortune”, recorded since the 15th century.

gesundheit.text: Middle High German gesuntheit, Old High German gisunt and gisunti “being unharmed”, recorded since the 8th century.

tag.text: Middle High German tac, tag, Old High German tag, recorded since the 8th century; Old Saxon dag. From Germanic *dagaz (the heat, later: the day), Indo-European *agh- (= “day”) + an unclear d-.

morgen.text: This adverb of time is an inherited word. Via the Middle High German forms morgen and morgene (compare Middle Low German morgen and Middle Dutch morgen), it goes back to Old High German morgane, recorded since the 9th century.

vormittag.text: Compound of the preposition vor and the noun Mittag.

mittag.text: Earlier forms of Mittag are Old High German mittitag, found in manuscripts from the 12th century, the older form mittilatag, which existed until the 8th century, and Middle High German mittetac.

nachmittag.text: Compound of the preposition nach and the noun Mittag.

abend.text: The origin is unclear; probably from Indo-European *epi – after, behind, close to; then Old High German āband, Middle High German ābent.

nacht.text: From Middle High German naht, Old High German naht, recorded since the 8th century.

woche.text: Middle High German woche, Old High German wehha, wohha, Germanic * wikōn “week”; recorded since the 8th century.

wochenende.text: Compound of the nouns Woche and Ende, with the linking element -n. Since the First World War, “modelled on English weekend, also ›free time from Saturday (morning or afternoon) until Sunday evening‹, today mostly ›from Friday afternoon on‹, also ›time off work‹”.

fruehstueck.text: 15th century, late Middle High German vrüestücke and vruostücke; Middle High German morgenbrōt. Literally the piece of bread eaten early in the morning.

mittagessen.text: Compound of the nouns Mittag and Essen.

abendessen.text: From Middle High German ābenteʒʒen, a compound of ābent (Abend) and eʒʒen (Essen).

pause.text: Middle High German pūse, borrowed in the 14th century from Old French pause. This goes back to Latin pausa ‘pause’ and further to Greek παῦσις ‘rest, repose’.

arbeit.text: Middle High German arebeit “hardship, suffering, effort”, Old High German arabeit, arabeiti, Germanic arbaiþi- “work, toil”. Related to Erbe, possibly related to arm and to Old Church Slavonic rabota (toil, slavery). Recorded since the 8th century.

job.text: Borrowed in the 20th century from English job, with the same meaning. Further origin unclear.

firma.text: Borrowed in the 18th century from Italian firma “legally valid signature on a business agreement”, which goes back to Latin firmare “to fasten, secure, strengthen”.

buero.text: Borrowed in the 17th century from French bureau, with the same meaning. Originally it meant “coarse woollen cloth”.

chef.text: Taken from French chef in the 17th century. The French word goes back to Latin caput “head”.

chefin.text: Feminine form made from the masculine Chef with the suffix -in.

kollege.text: Borrowed in the 16th century from Latin collega “fellow official”, literally “fellow delegate”. It is made of the prefix con- (com-) “with, together” and the noun lex “law”. So a Kollege was originally a person who lives under the same law as oneself.

kollegin.text: Feminine form made from the stem of Kollege with the suffix -in.

lehrer.text: Gothic laisareis, Old High German lêrari, Middle High German lêrære, lêrer. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

lehrerin.text: Feminine form made from Lehrer with the suffix -in.

koch.text: Recorded since the 9th century. From Middle High German koch; Old High German choch, koh, kohho; from Late Latin coco, with the same meaning; from Latin coquus, formed from the verb coquere (to cook).

kellner.text: Kellner has had its present meaning since the 18th century; before that it meant ‘head of the storehouse’. It is recorded since the 9th century and goes back to Middle High German kelnære or kelner (cellar master, manager of the vineyards). There was also the variant kellerer and, in Early New High German, the form keller.

fahrer.text: Formed from the stem of the verb fahren with the suffix -er.

ingenieur.text: From Latin gignere “to produce” and ingenium “invention, cleverness, war machine”; then Italian ingegnere “military engineer”, French ingénieur. Later used for jobs like shipbuilder and finally for technical experts in general. Borrowed in the 16th century.

polizist.text: The word appears in German in the mid-19th century. It was formed from Polizei by replacing the suffix -ei with the suffix -ist.

student.text: Middle High German studente, borrowed from the Latin participle studēns, studentis of the verb studēre “to make an effort, to study”. The word is recorded since the 15th century.

gloss.sich bemühen, studieren: to make an effort, to study

praktikum.text: A new word with a Latin form, made in the 20th century from Praktik.

gehalt.text: Late Middle High German gehalt, a noun from the verb gehalten “to hold firmly”, recorded since the 15th century. It first meant “precious metal content”, then generally “share”.

feierabend.text: Middle High German vīrābent = the evening before a holiday. Present meaning since the 16th century.

urlaub.text: From Middle High German “urloup”, Old High German “urloub”, an old noun related to erlauben. The word is recorded since the 8th century. Original meaning: “permission to leave”.

schule.text: Middle High German schuol, schuole, Old High German scuola (recorded since the 9th century). Probably borrowed in the 6th century from Late Latin schola, Latin schola “rest, school, lessons”. This comes from Greek σχολή “lecture hall, (learned) conversation, leisure, rest, school, lecture”.

klasse.text: Klasse was borrowed in the 16th century from Latin classis “division”, from the verb calare “to call together, summon”. So the meaning was really a calling-together, and from that: summons, levy, “military unit”; then the meaning “group with shared features”.

kurs.text: Borrowed in the 15th century from Latin cursus “run, course”. In the meaning of travel route, influenced by French cours and Dutch koers, recorded since the 16th century.

uebung.text: Formed from the verb üben with the suffix -ung.

pruefung.text: Noun formed from the stem of the verb prüfen with the suffix -ung.

test.text: Borrowed in the early 20th century from English test. This goes back through Old French test “earthen pot, crucible” to Latin testum “dish, bowl”. An earlier Middle High German test “crucible, pot”, borrowed from Old French, stayed in use until the 19th century.

note.text: The word developed from Latin nota (“written sign, explanatory note, mark, sign”), but its deeper origin remains uncertain.

buch.text: From Middle High German buoch, Old High German buoh, (a wooden writing tablet made of) beech, Germanic *bok-o. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

heft.text: Formed back from the verb heften, recorded since the mid-18th century (at first mostly masculine).

stift.text: Middle High German stift, steft, Old High German stift, recorded since the 11th century.

bleistift.text: “first in 1653 in Nuremberg as Bleystefft, shortened from Bleyweißstefft”.

papier.text: Borrowed in the 15th century from Latin papȳrum, which itself goes back to Greek πάπυρος.

tafel.text: Middle High German tavel, tavele, Old High German tavala, tabela, borrowed in the 8th century from early Romance tavola, which goes back to Latin tabula “board”.

wort.text: Middle High German wort, Old High German wort, Germanic *wurda- “word”, Indo-European *werdo- “word”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

satz.text: From Middle High German saz, also satz “saying, decision, law, position, decree, contract”, derived from Setzen: what is set down, in the Middle High German sense of “arrangement of words, a saying put into words”.

frage.text: Middle High German vrāg/vrāge, Old High German frāga, recorded since the 9th century (next to the older frāha, 8th century). It goes back to the West Germanic verb fræg-æ- “to ask”.

antwort.text: Middle High German antwürte, antwurt, Old High German antwurti, Germanic *anda-wurd-ja-, literally “counter-word”, from *anda “against”, compare ent-, Antlitz, and *wurda- (Wort). Originally neuter like Wort. In Old High German there was also a parallel feminine form antwurtī; in Middle High German both sounded the same.

beispiel.text: Late Middle High German bīspil (bispil), reshaped by folk etymology after Spiel, from Middle and Old High German bīspel = “instructive story”, “parable”, “proverb”, from bi (bei) and Middle and Old High German spel = “story” (originally “[meaningful] speech”).

universitaet.text: Borrowed in the 14th century from Latin universitas “the all-embracing whole”.

freizeit.text: Formed by merging freie Zeit, that is, a compound of frei and Zeit. First recorded in writing in 1823.

hobby.text: Borrowed in the 20th century from English hobby, with the same meaning. It really means “small horse, favourite horse”. The origin is not clear; possibly from Middle English hobin “small horse”, a variant of the name Robert or Robin.

sport.text: Borrowed in the 19th century from English sport, a short form of disport “diversion, amusement”. This goes back to Old French desport, déport “amusement”, a noun from the Old French verb deporter “to amuse oneself”.

fussball.text: Structure: a compound of the nouns Fuß and Ball.

musik.text: Borrowed into Old High German since the 9th century through Latin (ars) musica from Ancient Greek μουσική τέχνη “art of the Muses”.

film.text: Borrowed in the 19th century from English film.

kino.text: Shortened from Kinematograph, recorded since the 20th century.

konzert.text: Borrowed in the 17th century from Italian concerto, with the same meaning. The word really means: agreement, harmony. It is formed from the verb concertare = to agree, arrange; from Church Latin concertare = to work together; from Latin concertare = to compete; from the prefix con- = with.

party.text: Party was taken into German from English party, with the same meaning. This goes back to French partie ‘part, group of people/things’, which was formed from the verb partir.

spiel.text: Middle and Old High German spil, recorded since the 9th century. Further origin unknown.

karte.text: Borrowed in the 14th century from French carte “stiff sheet”; from Latin charta = “sheet of Egyptian papyrus”, from Greek chartēs, with the same meaning, probably a loanword from Arabic.

schwimmbad.text: Compound of the stem of the verb schwimmen and the noun Bad.

park.text: Borrowed in the 18th century from French parc, which goes back to Medieval Latin parricus (enclosure, fenced area). “In the meaning »Gehege« the word had already been borrowed earlier.”

caf.text: Taken in the 18th century from French café, with the same meaning. It was used for “coffee” and also, by extension, for a coffee house. It comes through Italian caffé from Turkish kahve, with the same meaning, from Arabic qahwā, probably named after the region of Kaffa, the home of the coffee plant.

restaurant.text: Borrowed in the 19th century from French restaurant.

zeitung.text: Since around 1300 zīdunge “message, news” is recorded. It goes back to Middle Low German/Middle Dutch tīdinge “news”. According to Kluge, a printed sheet of news first appeared in 1502 in Augsburg with the title “Newe zeytung”. Newspapers in today’s sense exist since the 17th century.

zentrum.text: From Middle High German zenter, in the 13th century from Latin centrum, “centre, axis point, hub”, from Ancient Greek κέντρον, “centre of a circle”, literally “goad (the fixed leg of a compass), thorn”; from an Indo-European root *kent-, “to prick”.

platz.text: Middle High German blaz, plaz, borrowed in the 13th century from Latin placea, partly through French place. This comes from Classical Latin platea, and that in turn from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateia, street, open public space). Some of today’s meanings come partly from English influence.

bank.text: Middle High German banc, Old High German bank, Germanic *banki- “bench”, recorded since the 9th century.

post.text: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian posta “post”. It was originally the name for the relay stations of the postal system; from Latin posita “fixed, placed”.

kirche.text: Kirche goes back to Old High German kirihha, found in the 8th century, and Middle High German kirche.

museum.text: Museum goes back through Latin museum ‘place for scholarly work’ to Ancient Greek μουσεῖον ‘temple of the Muses, seat of the Muses’. It was borrowed into German in the 16th century. Here it first meant ‘study room’, then in the 17th century ‘collection of art and antiquities’.

gloss.Musentempel, Musensitz: temple of the Muses, seat of the Muses

bibliothek.text: Borrowed in the 16th century from Latin bibliotheca (for “library”), which goes back to Greek βιβλιοθήκη, with the same meaning; from Greek βιβλίον for “book” and Greek θήκη for “container”.

hotel.text: Borrowed in the 18th century from the French noun hôtel. Related to Hospital.

polizei.text: The word is recorded in German since the 14th century. It was borrowed from Latin policia “state administration”, which goes back to Greek politeia, with the same meaning.

flughafen.text: Compound of the nouns Flug and Hafen.

haltestelle.text: Compound of the stem of the verb halten and the noun Stelle, with the linking sound -e-.

parkplatz.text: The word is recorded since the 1920s.

bruecke.text: Middle High German brücke, brucke, brügge, Old High German brugga, Germanic *brugjo; compare English bridge, Swedish brygga. Probably from a collective form *bhruk, *bhruko (compare Prügel), from an Indo-European root *bhrw, *bhru, “plank, simple bridge, trunk”; compare Swedish bro.

ecke.text: Middle High German ecke, Old High German egga, Germanic *agjō “sharpness, edge”, recorded since the 11th century. As part of the compound eggibug “turn-off” it already appears in the 8th century.

weg.text: Middle High German wec, Old High German wec or weg “path, road, walk, journey”, Germanic *wega- “track”, from Indo-European *u̯eg̑h- “to move, pull, travel”.

richtung.text: The word is recorded since the second half of the 18th century. Middle High German “richtunge” and Old High German “richtunga” had a different meaning: “court, judgement”.

plan.text: Borrowed in the early 18th century from French plan “draft, ground area, floor plan”. From the second half of the 18th century it also means “intention, project”. It goes back ultimately to Latin plantare “to plant”.

dorf.text: Middle High German dorf, Old High German dorf, Germanic *þurpa-, Indo-European *trěb- “timber building, building, dwelling”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

gebaeude.text: Middle High German gebūwede, Old High German gibūida, gibūwlida, gibūidi “building”, recorded since the 13th century.

auto.text: A short form of the compound Automobil, created in the early 20th century. Automobil was formed with the Greek prefix auto- “self-”.

bus.text: It is a short form of »Omnibus«, taken from its last syllable. In the 19th century it became common first in England in the form bus, then in the early 20th century also in Germany and France.

zug.text: Middle High German zuc, zug, Old High German zug ‘movement, pulling’, West Germanic tugi- ‘pull’. Recorded since the 11th century, according to Pfeifer since the 9th century. A noun formed from ziehen.

bahn.text: Middle High German ban or bane “track, way”, and like Old High German bana “death, ruin”, Gothic banja “blow, wound, ulcer”. Today’s meaning probably comes from clearing a way through the forest by cutting.

u-bahn.text: Abbreviation, short form (more exactly: a partial short form) of Untergrundbahn.

s-bahn.text: Abbreviation, short form of Schnellbahn or Stadtschnellbahn, in some regions also Stadtbahn.

strassenbahn.text: Compound of the noun Straße, the linking element -n and the noun Bahn.

taxi.text: Borrowed in the 1920s from English taxi or French taxi, a shortened form of taximètre (a device that calculates the price of a taxi ride). The word is based on Latin taxa “fee”.

fahrkarte.text: Compound of the stem of the verb fahren and Karte.

ticket.text: Borrowed from English ticket in the 18th century. The word goes back through Old French estiquier, estequier “to stick in” to a Germanic word.

fahrplan.text: Compound of the stem of the verb fahren and Plan.

gleis.text: Gleis goes back to late Middle High German geleise (wheel track, trodden path), found in the 14th century. This is a collective form of the Middle High German noun leis or leise (track), which has disappeared in modern German.

ausgang.text: Middle and Old High German ūʒganc, recorded since around 800.

eingang.text: Middle High German īnganc, inganc, Old High German ingang, recorded since the 8th century.

ampel.text: »Ampel« is a loanword from Latin, recorded since the 10th century. Its Old High German forms were ampulla and ampla, which became ampulle and ampel in Middle High German (compare also Middle Low German apolle, appolle, appulle, Middle Dutch ampulle, appulle).

verkehr.text: Noun formed from verkehren, recorded since the first half of the 18th century, first in the sense of “trade”.

stau.text: According to Duden, formed back from the verb stauen, which comes from Middle Low German stowen “to make stand, to place”. Recorded since the 18th century.

benzin.text: Originally the name the German chemist Mitscherlich gave in 1833 to the hydrocarbon that J. von Liebig later called Benzol. The term Benzin then came to mean the fuel.

motorrad.text: Compound of the nouns Motor and Rad.

reise.text: Middle High German reis(e), Old High German reisa, derived from the common Germanic verb *reis-a- “to rise”, “to go up”. Recorded since the 9th century.

koffer.text: Borrowed in the 14th century from French coffre “suitcase, box, chest”; from Latin cophinus “basket”, from Ancient Greek κόφινος, with the same meaning. Further origin unknown. Today’s meaning is recorded since the 18th century.

tasche.text: Middle High German tasche, tesche, Old High German tasca, recorded since the 9th century. Further origin unclear.

pass.text: Shortened in the 17th century from paßbrif and paßport, which are already mentioned in the 15th century. paßport is borrowed from the French noun passeport “permission to pass through”.

ausweis.text: The word is recorded since around 1600.

doppelzimmer.text: Compound of the stem of the adjective doppelt and the noun Zimmer.

rezeption.text: Borrowed in the 16th century from Medieval Latin receptio, a noun from the Latin verb recipere (= to accept, take in, receive).

gepaeck.text: Middle High German gepac, recorded since the 14th century, with umlaut since the 16th century.

strand.text: The word goes back to Middle High German strant, which Baltic Sea sailors borrowed from a Scandinavian language at the end of the 13th century.

meer.text: From Middle High German mer, Old High German mer(i), Germanic *marja, Indo-European *mori or *mari, “swamp, lake”, probably from Indo-European *mer-, “to shine”.

see.text: Recorded since the 8th century. Middle High German sē, Old High German sēo, Proto-Germanic *saiwiz ‘lake, sea’; also Dutch zee, English sea, Gothic saiws. Perhaps a noun from the verb *sīχwanan ‘to strain, to trickle’, which gave seihen.

berg.text: From Middle High German berc, from Old High German berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰos “height”. Recorded since the 9th century.

insel.text: Middle High German insel, insele, older isule, insule, Old High German isila, borrowed from the Latin noun insula. Recorded since the 9th century, in the new form since the 13th century.

ausland.text: In common use since the 18th century; formed back from Ausländer in the 17th century. Middle High German ūʒlant “estate lying outside the district boundary”, Old High German ūʒlenti “shore”.

heimat.text: Middle High German heimôt(e), heimuot(e), Old High German heimôti, derived from heim (today Heim) with the suffix -ôti, as in Heirat, Armut, Kleinod and so on. According to Kluge, this suffix is unclear. The word is recorded since the 11th century.

grenze.text: Middle High German “greniz, grenize”, borrowed from Slavic (compare for example Polish granica “border”). The word is recorded since the 13th century.

souvenir.text: Borrowed in the 18th century from French souvenir, a noun from the verb souvenir “to remember”, which goes back to Latin subvenire “to occur to someone, to come to mind”.

gloss.einfallen, in die Gedanken kommen: to occur to someone, to come to mind

aussicht.text: Noun related to aussehen. In the first meaning already recorded in 1709, in the second meaning since the mid-18th century.

uhr.text: Late Middle High German ur(r), taken in the 14th century from Middle Low German ūr(e), Middle Dutch ure. The Low German/Dutch word goes back through Old French (h)ore and Latin hora to Greek ὥρα “hour, time”.

stunde.text: Middle High German “stunde, stunt”, Old High German “stunta”, common Germanic (not recorded in Gothic) “*stundō” “period of time, hour”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

minute.text: Borrowed in the 15th century from Late Latin minuta, from Latin minutus “reduced, very small”, the past participle of minuere “to make smaller”, related to minus “less”.

sekunde.text: Borrowed in the second half of the 15th century from Medieval Latin secundum “sixtieth part of a minute”.

monat.text: It is an inherited word. It goes back through Middle High German mānōt to the Old High German forms mānōd, mānōth, recorded since the 8th century.

jahr.text: From Middle High German jār, Old High German jār, Germanic *jæra- “year”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

datum.text: From Latin datum “given”, recorded since the 13th century; used as a noun on its own only later.

zeit.text: Middle High German zît, Old High German zît “something divided off”, from Proto-Germanic, 8th century (compare English tide, Dutch tijd, Old Saxon tid); further from Proto-Indo-European *di-ti- “division of time”, from the stem *da- “to divide”, from which the following word groups also come, among others.

montag.text: From Middle High German māntag, mōntac, mēntac, Old High German mānotag (day of the moon). A loan translation of Latin dies Lunae (day of the moon goddess Luna), which goes back to Greek ἡμέρα Σελήνης “day of the moon goddess Selene”. The word is recorded since the 11th century.

gloss.Tag der Mondgöttin Selene: day of the moon goddess Selene

dienstag.text: Old Germanic Zi(e)stag (from the old German god Zio) or Old Norse Tysdagr (from the god Tyr). Another explanation: derived from a Latinised form of the Germanic war god Mars Thingsus (“Mars of the Thing”, the assembly).

mittwoch.text: Recorded since around 1000; originally feminine. Middle High German mittewoche, Old High German mittawehha, a compound of mitta ‘middle’ and wehha ‘week’. A loan translation of Church Latin media hebdomas ‘the middle of the week’, which gave Sicilian meazeamda and Vegliote misedma.

donnerstag.text: Middle High German donerstac, Old High German Donares tag, from the Germanic god Donar and Tag.

freitag.text: The word goes back through Middle High German vrītac to the Old High German forms frīatag, frījatag and frijetag, recorded since the 9th century.

samstag.text: Recorded since the 9th century, in the Middle High German forms samztac, sameztac and the Old High German forms sambaztag, samiztag. The Old High German forms come from Latin sabbatum, which in turn comes from New Testament Greek σάββατον.

sonntag.text: From Middle High German sunnentac, sunnetac, suntac, Old High German sunnūntag “day of the sun”. A loan translation of Latin dies solis, which goes back to Ancient Greek ἡμέρα Ἡλίου “day of the sun god Helios”. The word is recorded since the 9th century.

gloss.Tag des Sonnengottes Helios: day of the sun god Helios

wetter.text: Middle High German weter, wetter, Old High German wetar, Germanic *wedra- “weather”, recorded since the 8th century.

sonne.text: Middle High German sunne, Old High German sunna, Gothic sunno, Indo-European *sun- or *su̯en- “sun”, from *su̯el- “to smoulder, burn”.

regen.text: Middle High German regen < Old High German regan < Germanic *regna-, recorded since the 8th century. Further origin unclear.

schnee.text: From Middle High German snē, Old High German snēo “snow”. This common Germanic word, reconstructed for Proto-Germanic as *snaigwa- (see English snow, Dutch sneeuw, Swedish snö), comes from an Indo-European root *sneigh- “to snow”, “to stick”, “to stay lying”.

wind.text: Old High German wint, Old Saxon wind, Old English wind, Old Norse vindr, Gothic winds < Germanic *wenda- (masculine) “wind”.

wolke.text: Middle High German wolken, Old High German wolkan, Germanic *wulkna-, recorded since the 8th century. The word possibly goes back to the Indo-European root *u̯elg- “damp, wet”. It was originally neuter; only since late Middle High German is “die Wolke” feminine.

himmel.text: Middle High German “himel”, Old High German “himil” “cover, ceiling”, Germanic *“himena-” “sky, heaven”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

temperatur.text: From Latin temperatura “right mixture, right proportion”.

grad.text: Middle High German grāt, Old High German grād “step, rank”, borrowed around the year 1000 from Latin gradus “step, stage, gradation, rank”.

fruehling.text: Noun formed from the adjective früh with the suffix -ling, created in the 15th century.

sommer.text: Sommer comes through Middle High German sumer, Old High German sumar, like English summer and Dutch zomer, from Germanic *sumera- (summer). The word is recorded since the 8th century.

herbst.text: Middle High German herb(e)st, Old High German herbist(o), Germanic *harbista- “autumn”, earlier probably “harvest”; from Indo-European *karp- “to harvest”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

winter.text: From Middle High German winter, winder, Old High German wintar, Germanic *went-r- “winter”. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

jahreszeit.text: Compound of the nouns Jahr and Zeit with the linking element -es.

gewitter.text: Middle High German gewitter(e), Old High German giwittiri, West Germanic *ga-wedr-ja- “thunderstorm”, recorded since the 9th century.

nebel.text: Middle High German nebel, Old High German nebul, Old Saxon neƀal “fog, darkness”, Anglo-Saxon nifol, Old Icelandic nifl-heimr, njōl “darkness, night” < Germanic *neƀla-, *niƀula-. The Germanic word is related to Ancient Greek νεφέλη “cloud, fog” and Latin nebula “haze, fog, cloud”.

tier.text: From Middle High German tier, dier, Old High German tior, tëor, Germanic *deuza- “wild animal”. Probably from the Indo-European root *dheu- “to blow, breathe”, in the sense of “breathing being, living creature” (like Latin animal “animal” from anima “soul”). The word is recorded since the 8th century.

hund.text: From Old High German hunt < Indo-European *kwon-, which also gave Greek κύων (kýōn) (see also zynisch) and Latin canis (dog) (see also Kanarische Inseln).

katze.text: The name of this animal is an old but fairly late ‘wandering word’. Since the end of antiquity it appears in almost all European and some non-European languages, but its origin and how it spread are unknown.

vogel.text: From Middle High German vogel, Old High German fogal, fugal, Germanic *fugla-, recorded since the 8th century. A link to the root of fliegen has been suggested.

pferd.text: Recorded since the 9th century. Middle High German pfärvrit, pfärit, pfert, Old High German pfarifrit, pfärfrit, borrowed from Late Latin paraveredus ‘(extra) post horse’, a blend of Greek πάριππος with Gaulish verēdus ‘courier horse’ (compare Welsh gorwydd).

kuh.text: Middle and Old High German kuo, from Indo-European *gu̯ō̌u- “cattle”, perhaps imitating a sound. Recorded since the 8th century.

schwein.text: Old High German swin, from Proto-Germanic *swinan (compare also English swine, Dutch zwijn, Swedish svin and so on). Further from the Proto-Indo-European stem *su- (compare German Sau, Latin suinus and sus, Russian свин and свинья, Latvian sivens, Irish suig and so on).

maus.text: Middle High German, Old High German, Old Saxon, Old English, Old Franconian mūs, Old Norse mús, from Germanic *mūs-, from Indo-European *mūs-; compare Ancient Greek μυς- and Sanskrit mus-.

baum.text: Middle and Old High German boum, Old Norse baðmr, Gothic bagms. Origin uncertain.

blume.text: Middle High German bluome (feminine/masculine); Old High German bluoma (feminine), bluomo (masculine); Proto-Germanic *blōmô (masculine). It is based on the Indo-European verb root *bhēl, in a reduced form with the suffix o: *bhlo- “to thrive, bloom”, from which Latin flos “flower” also comes.

gras.text: Old and Middle High German gras, common Germanic *grasa- ‘grass, herb’, recorded since the 8th century. Linked with Latin gramen ‘grass’, from which Indo-European *ghrəs- ‘grass, plant shoot’ can be reconstructed, going back to *gher(ə)- ‘to stick out (of plant shoots, thorns, raised ground)’.

wald.text: From Middle High German walt, from Old High German wald (8th century), from Proto-Germanic *walþuz, from Proto-Indo-European *weltos. For further related words, see *weltos.

fluss.text: Old High German fluʒ “flowing”, recorded since the 8th century, Middle High German vluʒ; since the 16th century “flowing body of water”.

wiese.text: From Middle High German wise, Old High German wisa, recorded since the 8th century. Further origin unclear.

natur.text: Recorded since the 9th century. Middle High German natūre; Old High German natūra; from Latin natura, literally “birth”; from nasci (nātus sum) “to be born”.

luft.text: Middle High German luft, Old High German luft, Germanic *luftu- “air”, recorded since the 8th century.

erde.text: Middle High German erde, from Old High German erda, from the 8th century.

feld.text: From veld, feld; originally “something flat” or “something wide”. Recorded since the 8th century.

stein.text: The noun Stein belongs to the basic vocabulary, meaning a natural, solid, hard body made of minerals, rock. It is recorded since the 8th century and comes from Old High German stein, Middle High German stein, Old Saxon stēn, Middle Low German stēn.

blatt.text: Middle High German blat, Old High German blat, Germanic *blada- ‘leaf’. The word is recorded since the 8th century.

amt.text: Derived from Middle High German ambt or ambahte; Old High German ambaht, “servant, follower”; Gallo-Latin ambactus; related to Germanic ombud.

behoerde.text: From the old word behören, Middle High German behœren = to belong to. It really means the place or (official) office where something belongs. Recorded since the 17th century.

formular.text: A learned formation of the 16th century from Latin formularium “what belongs to legal formulas”, from Latin formula “law, legal formula, rule, regulation”, literally “little form, little rule”, a diminutive of Latin forma “form, shape”.

anmeldung.text: Noun formed from the stem of anmelden with the suffix -ung.

aufenthalt.text: Middle High German ūfenthalt “stay, lodging, maintenance”.

visum.text: Borrowed in the 20th century from Latin visum “seen”.

geburtsurkunde.text: Compound of Geburt, the linking element -s and Urkunde.

staatsangehoerigkeit.text: The word is recorded since the 19th century.

familienstand.text: Compound of the noun Familie, the linking element -n and the noun Stand.

geburtsort.text: Compound of the words Geburt, the linking element -s and Ort.

mitarbeiter.text: Formed from the stem of mitarbeiten with the suffix -er.

nummer.text: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian numero, which goes back to Latin numerus “numeral sign”.

oeffnungszeit.text: Compound of the nouns Öffnung and Zeit with the linking element -s.

dokument.text: Borrowed in the 16th century from Medieval Latin documentum ‘document that proves something’, which goes back to Latin documentum ‘proof, lesson’.

kopie.text: Recorded since the 14th century. Borrowed from Medieval Latin copia = “written copy”; from Latin copia = “supply, abundance, plenty”; from the prefix con-, co- = “with” and the noun ops = “power”.

gebuehr.text: Middle High German gebür(e), Old High German giburi, literally = what is due to someone, what falls to them; related to gebühren.
